## Messaging (cereal)

### 3.1 What cereal is

`cereal/` is openpilot's inter-process messaging layer: a [Cap'n Proto](https://capnproto.org/) schema (`cereal/log.capnp`, plus imported `car.capnp`/`custom.capnp`/`legacy.capnp`) defining every message type exchanged between daemons, paired with a pub/sub transport (`msgq`, a shared-memory message queue with a ZMQ-compatible fallback — `cereal/messaging/bridge_zmq.cc`, `msgq_to_zmq.cc`) and a small Python convenience API (`cereal/messaging/__init__.py`) that essentially every process in the stack (UI, controls, sim, replay tooling) imports as `cereal.messaging` / `messaging`.

### 3.2 Schema location and categories — confirmed structure, not exhaustively cataloged per scope

- **`cereal/log.capnp`** (`@0xf3b1f17e25a4285b`) — the main schema, defining the top-level `Event` union (implicit — referenced as `log.Event` throughout the Python API) and 61 `struct` definitions (`grep -c '^struct '` = 61) covering: vehicle/driving state (`OnroadEvent`, `SelfdriveState`, `ControlsState`, `DrivingModelData`, `ModelDataV2`, `LongitudinalPlan`, `LateralPlan`, `RadarState`, `DriverAssistance`, `DriverMonitoringState`, `DriverStateV2`), device/hardware telemetry (`DeviceState`, `PandaState`, `PeripheralState`, `SensorEventData`, `GpsLocationData`, `GNSSMeasurements`/`UbloxGnss`/`QcomGnss`, `CanData`, `Touch`), localization (`LiveLocationKalman`, `LivePose`, `LiveCalibrationData`, `LiveParametersData`, `LiveTorqueParametersData`, `LiveDelayData`), camera/vision plumbing (`FrameData`, `Thumbnail`, `EncodeIndex`/`EncodeData`, `CameraOdometry`), system/process management (`InitData`, `Boot`, `ManagerState`, `UploaderState`, `ProcLog`, `Sentinel`), UI/audio (`UIDebug`, `SoundPressure`, `AudioData`, `AudioFeedback`, `UserBookmark`, `DebugAlert`), navigation (`NavInstruction`, `NavRoute`, `MapRenderState`, `NavModelData`), and a generic `Map(Key,Value)` template. Several structs are marked `DEPRECATED` in-name (e.g. `LiveTracksDEPRECATED`, `DriverStateDEPRECATED`, `LiveMapDataDEPRECATED`) but still defined for backward log-format compatibility.
- **`cereal/car.capnp`** — in this checkout, this file is literally a one-line symlink pointing at `../opendbc_repo/opendbc/car/car.capnp` (confirmed: `cereal/car.capnp` contains exactly the text `../opendbc_repo/opendbc/car/car.capnp`, 37 bytes, checked out as a plain-text file rather than a real symlink because of `core.symlinks=false`/Windows). **This is a notable structural fact**: the car-interface schema (`CarState`, `CarControl`, `CarParams`, `CarOutput`, button/event enums, etc.) has moved out of `cereal/` proper and now lives in the `opendbc` submodule/subtree (`opendbc_repo/`), with `cereal/car.capnp` kept only as a compatibility redirect so `import "car.capnp"` statements inside `log.capnp` keep resolving. Any documentation describing `car.capnp` as authored directly under `cereal/` is stale for this fork.
- **`cereal/custom.capnp`** — explicitly reserved empty structs (`CustomReserved0`..`CustomReserved5`) for forks to add custom message types without breaking wire-compatibility with mainline `log.capnp`; comments instruct forks to rename (but not renumber) these when used (`cereal/custom.capnp:7-11`). **Uncertain** whether this fork (`openpilot-xnor-bis`) has actually populated any of these — not observed in the files read.
- **`cereal/legacy.capnp`** — presumably holds retired/renumbered struct definitions for wire compatibility (not read in full; out of scope for exhaustive review).
- **`cereal/services.py`** / **`services.h`** — the service registry: `SERVICE_LIST` maps every service name to a `Service(should_log, frequency_hz, decimation, queue_size)` tuple (`_services` dict, `cereal/services.py:24-`), e.g. `"can": (True, 100., 2053, QueueSize.BIG)`, `"controlsState": (True, 100., 10, QueueSize.MEDIUM)`. `QueueSize` (`:6-9`) is an `IntEnum` of shared-memory segment sizes: `BIG=10MB` (video/large AI output), `MEDIUM=2MB` (high-freq CAN/livestream), `SMALL=250KB` (default, most services). This registry is what `SubMaster`/`PubMaster` consult to size sockets and validate frequency expectations (§3.3).
- **`cereal/messaging/bridge.cc`**, **`bridge_zmq.cc`**, **`msgq_to_zmq.cc`**, **`socketmaster.cc`** — C++ transport plumbing bridging the native `msgq` shared-memory queue implementation with a ZMQ-based fallback (used e.g. for cross-machine debugging/replay streaming); not further inventoried per scope (interface-level only).

### 3.3 `cereal/messaging/__init__.py` — the Python pub/sub API

This is the single most widely-imported module in the whole codebase (every daemon shown in §1 and §2 uses it) — documented fully here per the assignment's instruction that it "needs to be documented once, accurately."

**Low-level helpers**:
- `pub_sock(endpoint)` / `sub_sock(endpoint, poller=None, addr="127.0.0.1", conflate=False, timeout=None)` (`:19-30`) — thin wrappers around the compiled `msgq` extension's `pub_sock`/`sub_sock`, auto-sizing the underlying shared-memory segment from `SERVICE_LIST[endpoint].queue_size` (falls back to `0`/default if the endpoint isn't a registered service).
- `new_message(service, size=None, **kwargs)` (`:42-54`) — builds a fresh capnp `Event` message: sets `valid=False` and `logMonoTime=int(time.monotonic()*1e9)` by default (overridable via kwargs), then `dat.init(service[, size])` to allocate the named union field (the `size` arg is for list-typed fields needing pre-sized allocation).
- `log_from_bytes(dat, struct=log.Event)` (`:37-39`) — deserializes raw bytes into a capnp reader, with `traversal_limit_in_words=NO_TRAVERSAL_LIMIT` (`2**64-1`) to disable capnp's default anti-DoS traversal cap (trusted-source assumption, since these are same-machine IPC messages, not untrusted network input).
- `drain_sock`/`recv_sock`/`recv_one`/`recv_one_or_none`/`recv_one_retry` (`:57-104`) — variations on receiving from a raw `SubSocket`: drain-all, latest-only (docstring recommends using `conflate=True` on the socket instead where possible), blocking-single, non-blocking-single, retry-until-received.

**`FrequencyTracker`** (`:107-147`) — internal helper embedded in `SubMaster` per-service; tracks a windowed (10x-period) and a recent (1x-period) `MovingAverage` of inter-message intervals, and derives a valid frequency band `[min_freq*0.8, max_freq*1.2]` from the service's nominal rate vs. the `SubMaster`'s poll/update rate (handles both "polled once, expect exactly that rate" and "background-updated, expect somewhere between half and double the target" cases, `:108-119`). `valid` property (`:137-147`) is true if either the long-window or recent-window average frequency falls in-band — this is what backs `SubMaster.freq_ok`.

**`SubMaster`** (`:150-247`) — the standard "subscribe to N services, get latest values, know what's stale" object used by essentially every consumer daemon (`ui_state.sm` in §1.7, `soundd`'s `sm`, `feedbackd`'s `sm`, sim bridge's `simulated_car.sm`, etc.):

| Constructor arg | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `services: List[str]` | Services to subscribe (required) |
| `poll: str \| None` | If set, only this one service drives the `Poller`'s blocking wait; all others are drained non-blockingly every `update()` call. If unset, *all* services are polled together. |
| `ignore_alive` / `ignore_avg_freq` / `ignore_valid` | Per-service opt-outs from the respective `all_*` health checks |
| `addr` | Socket bind address (`"127.0.0.1"` default — supports remote/replay scenarios) |
| `frequency` | Explicit override for the "expected update frequency" used by `FrequencyTracker`; mutually exclusive with `poll` (asserted, `:183`) — if `poll` is set, the polled service's own frequency is used instead |

Construction (`:151-196`): for each service, opens a `sub_sock` (registered with the shared `Poller` unless it's a non-polled service), seeds `self.data[s]` with a zeroed/default message of the right type (`new_message(s)`, falling back to `new_message(s, 0)` for list-typed fields that error on default-size init), and builds a `FrequencyTracker`. **Zero-frequency ("on-demand") services** — those with `SERVICE_LIST[s].frequency <= 1e-5` — are treated specially: they're presumed `alive`/`valid`/`freq_ok` from the start and never subjected to the staleness checks (`on_demand` dict, `:165-169`), since they're only published sporadically by design (e.g. one-shot/event messages).

Per-service state dicts, all keyed by service name and updated by `update_msgs()`:
| Dict | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `data[s]` | Latest received capnp reader for service `s` (also accessible via `sm[s]` / `sm['carState']` — `__getitem__`, `:198-199`) |
| `updated[s]` | True only on the frame a new message for `s` arrived (reset to all-`False` at the top of every `update_msgs()` call) |
| `seen[s]` | True forever once any message for `s` has ever arrived |
| `alive[s]` | True if a message arrived within `10 / frequency` seconds (10x the nominal period) — or always true for on-demand services, or (in `SIMULATION` mode) true once `seen` |
| `valid[s]` | Mirrors the last received message's own `valid` capnp field |
| `freq_ok[s]` | From `FrequencyTracker.valid`, or forced true under `SIMULATION` |
| `recv_time[s]` / `recv_frame[s]` / `logMonoTime[s]` | Wall-clock receipt time, `SubMaster.frame` counter value at receipt, and the message's own `logMonoTime` field |

- `update(timeout=100)` (`:204-212`): polls the shared `Poller` (100ms default timeout) for the polled services, non-blockingly drains every non-polled service's own socket, then calls `update_msgs(now, msgs)`.
- `update_msgs(cur_time, msgs)` (`:214-235`) — the core state-machine step: increments `self.frame`, resets `updated`, applies each received message to the corresponding dicts, then recomputes `alive`/`freq_ok` for every "static frequency" (non-on-demand) service based on elapsed time since last receipt — this recompute happens on *every* call regardless of whether that particular service had a new message, so staleness detection works even for services that silently stop publishing.
- `all_alive(service_list=None)` / `all_freq_ok(...)` / `all_valid(...)` / `all_checks(...)` (`:237-247`) — aggregate health predicates over a subset (default: all subscribed services) minus each check's own ignore-list; `all_checks` is the AND of all three and is the common "is everything healthy" gate used by control-loop daemons before engaging.

**`PubMaster`** (`:250-269`): `__init__(services)` opens one `pub_sock` per service name. `send(s, dat)` (`:256-259`) accepts either raw `bytes` or a capnp message builder (auto-calls `.to_bytes()`). `wait_for_readers_to_update(s, timeout, dt=0.05)` / `all_readers_updated(s)` (`:261-269`) poll the underlying msgq publisher's reader-ack tracking — useful in tests/tools that need to confirm a subscriber actually consumed a published message before proceeding (msgq supports this because it's a real shared-memory ring buffer with reader cursors, unlike fire-and-forget ZMQ PUB).

**Typical usage pattern** (as seen throughout §1/§2, e.g. `ui_state.py:35-59`, `soundd.py:149`, `feedbackd.py:14-15`):
```python
sm = messaging.SubMaster(['carState', 'selfdriveState', ...])
pm = messaging.PubMaster(['userBookmark'])
while True:
  sm.update(0)                       # 0 = non-blocking poll
  if sm.updated['selfdriveState']:
    ...
  msg = messaging.new_message('userBookmark', valid=True)
  pm.send('userBookmark', msg)
```

## Developer Tools

### 4.1 Overview

`tools/` hosts developer- and researcher-facing utilities that sit outside the on-device daemon set. Notably, **Qt/C++ is still very much in use here** (`tools/cabana/` is a full Qt widgets application — `mainwin.h`, `.cc` files with `.h` companions throughout, no raylib) even though the on-device driving UI (`selfdrive/ui/`, §1) has moved to raylib/Python — a useful architectural contrast when documenting "does this repo use Qt."

| Category | Directory | One-line summary |
|---|---|---|
| Drive replay | `tools/replay/` | C++ tool (`replay.cc`/`.h`, `main.cc`) that reads recorded route segments (rlogs) and republishes their cereal events live over the normal pub/sub bus, letting any real daemon consume a recorded drive as if it were live. See §4.2. |
| Simulator bridge | `tools/sim/` | Python bridge between the MetaDrive driving simulator and the real openpilot stack (see §4.3), plus keyboard/joystick manual-control input and Panda-in-the-loop-style car simulation. |
| CAN bus analyzer | `tools/cabana/` | Qt/C++ GUI (`mainwin`, `binaryview`, `signalview`, `messageswidget`, `historylog`, `videowidget`, `chart/`) for inspecting/decoding live or logged CAN traffic against DBC files, with synchronized video playback. |
| Plot visualization | `tools/plotjuggler/` | `juggle.py` launches PlotJuggler (a third-party time-series plotting tool) pre-configured (`layouts/`) to visualize cereal/rlog signals for tuning and debugging. |
| Manual control | `tools/joystick/` | `joystickd.py` — publishes synthetic `carControl`/testing inputs from a physical joystick or keyboard, for manually driving/testing without a real car. |
| Misc scripts | `tools/scripts/` | Standalone utility scripts: `adb_ssh.sh`/`setup_ssh_keys.py`/`ssh.py` (device SSH access helpers), `fetch_image_from_route.py`, `save_ubloxraw_stream.py`, `extract_audio.py`, `serial.sh`. |
| Car porting | `tools/car_porting/` | `auto_fingerprint.py`, `measure_steering_accuracy.py`, `test_car_model.py` — helpers for bringing up support for a new car model against opendbc. |
| Longitudinal tuning | `tools/longitudinal_maneuvers/` | `maneuversd.py` + report generators — scripted acceleration/braking maneuvers and MPC tuning-report generation for longitudinal control validation. |
| Clip capture | `tools/clip/` | `run.py` — records a UI clip (leverages the `RECORD`/ffmpeg pipeline in `system/ui/lib/application.py`, §1.3). |
| Body teleop | `tools/bodyteleop/` | Web-based remote teleoperation UI for comma body-type hardware (`static/` assets). |
| Camera / webcam streaming | `tools/camerastream/`, `tools/webcam/` | Stream device/webcam camera feeds for remote viewing or as a substitute video source. |
| Profiling | `tools/profiling/` | Wrappers/configs for `clpeak` (OpenCL benchmarking), Palanteer, Perfetto, `py-spy`, and Snapdragon profiling tools. |
| Shared libs | `tools/lib/` | Common Python helpers reused across the above (route/log loading utilities, etc.) — consumed by replay, cabana tooling, scripts. |

### 4.2 `tools/replay/` — drive replay

Entry point is the C++ `main.cc` driving the `Replay` class (`tools/replay/replay.h:35`), with `tools/replay/ui.py` providing a Python-side companion UI and `consoleui.cc` a terminal UI. Mechanically (confirmed from `replay.h`'s public interface): `Replay` is constructed with a `route` id, allow/block lists of service names to replay, an optional external `SubMaster*`, and a bitmask of `REPLAY_FLAGS` (`:17-28`) controlling behavior — `REPLAY_FLAG_DCAM`/`ECAM` (include driver/wide camera streams), `REPLAY_FLAG_NO_LOOP`, `REPLAY_FLAG_NO_FILE_CACHE`, `REPLAY_FLAG_QCAMERA` (use the low-res qcamera stream), `REPLAY_FLAG_NO_HW_DECODER`, `REPLAY_FLAG_NO_VIPC` (skip publishing video over VisionIPC), `REPLAY_FLAG_ALL_SERVICES`, `REPLAY_FLAG_BENCHMARK`.

`load()` fetches/validates the route via a `SegmentManager`+`Route` pair; `start(seconds)`/`seekTo(seconds, relative)`/`seekToFlag()`/`pause()` control playback position, backed by a dedicated `streamThread()` that walks decoded `Event`s and calls `publishMessage()`/`publishFrame()` — i.e. it re-publishes each historical cereal message and camera frame onto the live pub/sub bus (`PubMaster pm_`, optionally driving a caller-supplied `SubMaster* sm_` directly instead) at (adjustable via `setSpeed()`) the original relative timing, with a `CameraServer` component handling VisionIPC frame publishing for camera streams. A `Timeline` (`timeline.cc/.h`) indexes alert/event occurrences within the route for seeking-to-event support (`findAlertAtTime`), and segment loading/caching is handled by `SegmentManager` (`seg_mgr.cc/.h`) with a configurable `segmentCacheLimit`. In short: **replay reads recorded route segments and republishes them as live cereal traffic**, letting any real daemon (controlsd, UI, cabana, etc.) consume a past drive exactly as if it were happening now — the standard workflow for offline debugging and regression testing against real-world data.

### 4.3 `tools/sim/` — MetaDrive simulator bridge

Entry point `tools/sim/run_bridge.py:17` (`main()`): constructs a `MetaDriveBridge` (`tools/sim/bridge/metadrive/metadrive_bridge.py`, a concrete subclass of the abstract `SimulatorBridge` in `tools/sim/bridge/common.py:37`) and runs it as a **separate `multiprocessing.Process`** (`bridge.run(queue)` → `Process(target=bridge_keep_alive, ...)`, `common.py:70-88`), communicating with the parent process via a `multiprocessing.Queue` of `QueueMessage(type, info)` tuples for manual-control input (steer/throttle/brake/cruise-button/blinker/ignition/reset/quit commands, parsed in `_run()`, `common.py:132-161`).

The bridge's core loop (`SimulatorBridge._run`, `common.py:101-206`) is the actual openpilot↔simulator glue: it spins up a `SimulatedCar` (owns its own `SubMaster`/`PubMaster` pair emulating a real car's CAN interface toward the openpilot stack) and `SimulatedSensors` on separate `Ratekeeper`-driven threads (car state at 100Hz, camera frames at 20Hz via `rk_loop()`, `:30-34`), then in the main loop: reads manual-control queue messages, feeds the simulator's sensor state into openpilot via `SimulatedSensors.update()`, pulls openpilot's actuator commands back out of `carControl` (`sm['carControl'].actuators.accel/steeringAngleDeg`, converted to throttle/brake/steer via clip+scale, `:176-178`) whenever `selfdriveState.active` is true (falls back to the manual-control values otherwise), applies those controls to the simulator world (`world.apply_controls()`), and ticks the simulator world every `TICKS_PER_FRAME=5` main-loop iterations. It also force-engages openpilot automatically on startup once `selfdriveState.engageable` (alternating `DECEL_SET`/`MAIN` cruise-button presses, `:181-183`) so a scripted/headless simulation run doesn't need a human to press "set". It forces `AlphaLongitudinalEnabled=True` and calls `set_params_enabled()` at construction (`common.py:41-43`) so the simulated car always exercises full longitudinal control. In short: **the bridge runs the real openpilot process stack against a simulated car/world instead of real hardware**, translating simulator sensor output into the same cereal messages a real car would produce, and translating openpilot's `carControl` output back into simulator vehicle-dynamics commands — enabling closed-loop testing without a physical vehicle.

### 4.4 Remaining tool directories (one paragraph each)

**`tools/cabana/`** is comma's Qt-based CAN bus reverse-engineering and analysis tool: `mainwin.cc` hosts the main window, `binaryview`/`signalview` render raw CAN payload bits and decoded-signal views side by side, `messageswidget`/`historylog` list traffic and per-message value history, `chart/` plots signal values over time, `videowidget`/`cameraview.cc` sync a route's video against the CAN timeline, `dbc/` handles DBC file parsing/editing, `streams/` abstracts live-panda vs. replay-log vs. other CAN data sources, and `panda.cc` talks to physical Panda hardware directly for live capture.

**`tools/plotjuggler/`** (`juggle.py`) is a launcher/config layer around the third-party PlotJuggler application, with `layouts/` holding pre-built dashboard layouts for common openpilot signal groups, used for interactive time-series inspection of logged or live cereal data during tuning work.

**`tools/joystick/`** (`joystickd.py`, 81 lines) publishes control commands sourced from a physical joystick (or equivalent manual input), used for manually driving a car or the simulator while bypassing openpilot's normal planning/control stack — pairs with the `JoystickDebugMode` param (`common/params_keys.h`).

**`tools/scripts/`** is a flat collection of standalone one-off utilities: SSH/ADB access helpers (`adb_ssh.sh`, `setup_ssh_keys.py`, `ssh.py`, `serial.sh`) and data-extraction scripts (`fetch_image_from_route.py`, `save_ubloxraw_stream.py`, `extract_audio.py`) that don't belong to a larger tool package.

**`tools/car_porting/`** provides the workflow for adding support for a new car: `auto_fingerprint.py` derives a CAN fingerprint from captured traffic, `measure_steering_accuracy.py` and `test_car_model.py` validate a candidate car-interface implementation against opendbc conventions, with `examples/` showing reference implementations.

**`tools/longitudinal_maneuvers/`** runs and reports on scripted longitudinal (accel/brake) test maneuvers (`maneuversd.py`, `maneuver_helpers.py`) and generates MPC longitudinal-tuning comparison reports (`generate_report.py`, `mpc_longitudinal_tuning_report.py`) — used when tuning or validating the longitudinal control MPC.

**`tools/clip/`** (`run.py`) captures short video clips of the UI/onroad view, built on the `RECORD=1`/ffmpeg pipeline already present in `system/ui/lib/application.py` (§1.3) rather than reimplementing video capture.

**`tools/bodyteleop/`** serves a browser-based teleoperation interface (static HTML/JS assets) for remotely driving/controlling comma "body" hardware over a network connection.

**`tools/camerastream/`** and **`tools/webcam/`** provide, respectively, remote streaming of the device's own cameras (for viewing a live feed off-device) and using a PC webcam as a substitute input source for the vision pipeline during development without real device camera hardware.

**`tools/profiling/`** bundles configuration/wrapper scripts for several third-party profilers used against openpilot processes: `clpeak` (OpenCL device benchmarking), Palanteer and Perfetto (trace-based profilers), `py-spy` (sampling Python profiler, useful for attaching to running daemons without instrumentation), and Snapdragon-specific profiling tools (relevant to the `tici`/`tizi` on-device SoC).

**`tools/lib/`** holds shared Python helpers (route metadata/log-file access, etc.) reused by the replay tooling, cabana's Python-facing pieces, and assorted scripts — a common foundation rather than a standalone tool.

## Configuration (cross-cutting summary)

Confirmed from code across all subsystems above. openpilot has **no single config file** — configuration is spread across five mechanisms, in this precedence order for anything that appears in more than one:

1. **`Params` key-value store** (`common/params.py` → `common/params_pyx.pyx` → `common/params.h`/`.cc`) — the dominant mechanism. Each key is one file on disk (atomic write-via-rename+fsync), validated against a static ~190-entry registry in `common/params_keys.h` (unknown keys raise `UnknownKeyName`). Every key carries `ParamKeyFlag` bits (`CLEAR_ON_MANAGER_START`, `CLEAR_ON_ONROAD_TRANSITION`, `CLEAR_ON_OFFROAD_TRANSITION`, `CLEAR_ON_IGNITION_ON`, `DEVELOPMENT_ONLY`, and — per the UI/common agent — `DONT_LOG` exists in C++ but is missing from the Cython-exposed enum, a minor binding gap) that `system/manager/manager.py:manager_init`/`manager_thread` use to decide when to wipe state (§4.2 above). Persisted under `Paths.config_root()` (device) — survives reboots but not a factory reset; distinct from `Paths.persist_root()` (`/persist/`) which survives reflashes and holds the device private key + dongle ID.
2. **Environment variables**, read ad hoc throughout (`os.getenv`) rather than centrally validated: `USE_WEBCAM`, `NOBOARD`, `BLOCK`, `REPLAY`, `FAKESEND`, `BOARDD_LOOPBACK`, `BOARDD_SKIP_FW_CHECK`, `AGNOS_VERSION`, `STAGING_ROOT`, `QCOM_PRIORITY`, `LOG_ROOT`, `HANDLER_THREADS`, `BIG`, `PREPAREONLY`, thread-count vars in `launch_env.sh` (`OMP_NUM_THREADS` etc.). No single manifest of all recognized env vars exists; this document's subsystem sections list the ones found per-component.
3. **Command-line arguments** — minimal; mostly limited to dev tools (`tools/replay`, `tools/sim`) and the `--stream`/`--minimal`/`--verbose`/`--ccflags`/`--ubsan` flags to `SConstruct`/`encoderd`.
4. **`CarParams` (capnp message, also cached as a `Params` key)** — the per-drive, per-vehicle configuration blob computed once by `card.py` fingerprinting (confirmed §Car Interface above) and consumed by nearly every other daemon (`controlsd`, `plannerd`, `selfdrived`, `pandad`'s `PandaSafety`, etc.) as their source of vehicle-specific tuning (steer ratio, safety configs, longitudinal control availability, etc.). This is the one configuration surface that's fully schema-validated (capnp) rather than a loose string key-value store.
5. **Hardcoded constants** — pervasive (every subsystem section above has a constants table). Notable ones that function as de facto configuration: `V_CRUISE_MIN/MAX` (`selfdrive/car/cruise.py`), the longitudinal MPC cost weights (`selfdrive/controls/lib/longitudinal_mpc_lib/long_mpc.py`), `AGAIN_VERSION`/`STAGING_ROOT` defaults in `launch_env.sh`.

**Precedence when mechanisms overlap**: `Params` values generally win at runtime once set (e.g. `AGNOS_VERSION` env var default is only used if unset by `launch_env.sh`, not overridable by `Params`); process **enablement** (which of the 39 daemons run) is governed by `Params` + `CarParams` + env vars combined through the `should_run` predicates in `system/manager/process_config.py` (§4.4) — there is no single authority, each predicate hand-picks its own inputs.

## Dependencies (cross-cutting summary)

**Python** (`pyproject.toml`, `requires-python ">=3.12.3,<3.13"`, dependency-managed via `uv`, lockfile `uv.lock`): core dependencies split into (a) build tooling — `scons`, `pycapnp`, `Cython`, `cffi`, `setuptools`; (b) vendored native libraries pulled from `github.com/commaai/dependencies` at pinned tags — `bzip2`, `capnproto`, `eigen`, `ffmpeg`, `libjpeg`, `libyuv`, `zstd`, `ncurses`, `zeromq`, `libusb`, `git-lfs`, `gcc-arm-none-eabi` (this is how the project avoids depending on system-package versions of these — confirmed by the `SConstruct` "enforce a whitelist of system libraries" block, which only allows `EGL/GLESv2/GL/Qt5*/dl/drm/gbm/m/pthread` to come from the OS); (c) subsystem-specific — `sounddevice` (micd+soundd), `pyserial` (pigeond+qcomgpsd), `sympy` (rednose EKF codegen), `crcmod-plus` (CAN+qcomgpsd), `av`/`aiohttp`/`aiortc` (webrtcd/body teleop), `libusb1`/`spidev` (panda), `pyzmq`/`sentry-sdk`/`xattr` (logging), `PyJWT`/`json-rpc`/`websocket_client` (athena), `numpy>=2.0`. Test tooling: `pytest`, `pytest-cpp`, `pytest-subtests`, a patched fork of `pytest-xdist`, `pytest-asyncio`, `pytest-mock`.

**C/C++** (`SConstruct`): built via SCons against `bzip2, capnproto, eigen, ffmpeg, libjpeg, libyuv, ncurses, zeromq, zstd` (all vendored per above) plus an explicit system-library whitelist (`EGL, GLESv2, GL, Qt5Charts, Qt5Core, Qt5Gui, Qt5Widgets, dl, drm, gbm, m, pthread` — note Qt is only linked for `tools/cabana`, consistent with the UI-architecture finding above that the on-road UI itself is not Qt).

**Vendored sibling repositories** (out of exhaustive scope per the agreed scope, referenced at interface level throughout): `opendbc_repo` (per-car DBCs/CarInterface/safety firmware source — consumed by `selfdrive/car/`), `panda` (panda firmware/host lib — consumed by `selfdrive/pandad/`), `msgq_repo` (the actual SHM transport under `cereal.messaging`), `rednose_repo` (symbolic EKF codegen — consumed by `selfdrive/locationd/`), `tinygrad_repo` (the sole neural-net inference backend confirmed in `selfdrive/modeld/modeld.py` — no runtime ONNX/thneed path was found despite build-time ONNX export tooling existing), `teleoprtc_repo` (WebRTC teleoperation — consumed by `system/webrtc/`), `third_party` (prebuilt native libs for platforms without a `commaai/dependencies` build).

## Tests

**Framework**: `pytest` (+ `pytest-cpp` for native test binaries, `pytest-xdist` for parallelism, `pytest-asyncio`/`pytest-mock`). Root `conftest.py:11-19` excludes `selfdrive/test/process_replay/test_processes.py` and `test_regen.py` from normal collection (they need real routes/hardware) and ignores `selfdrive/debug/*.py`/`selfdrive/modeld/*.py` as non-test scripts. `pyproject.toml:126` holds `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`.

**Coverage footprint** (confirmed via directory survey): 64 `test_*.py` files across at least 23 test directories, spanning nearly every subsystem documented above — `selfdrive/car/tests`, `selfdrive/controls/tests`, `selfdrive/locationd/test`, `selfdrive/pandad/tests`, `selfdrive/selfdrived/tests`, `selfdrive/ui/tests` + `selfdrive/ui/mici/tests`, `system/athena/tests`, `system/camerad/test`, `system/hardware/tests` + `system/hardware/tici/tests`, `system/loggerd/tests`, `system/manager/test`, `system/qcomgpsd/tests`, `system/sensord/tests`, `system/ubloxd/tests`, `system/ui/lib/tests`, `system/updated/tests` + `system/updated/casync/tests`, `system/webrtc/tests`, `common/tests` + `common/transformations/tests`, plus top-level `selfdrive/test/` and `system/tests/`.

**openpilot's signature test methodology — process replay** (`selfdrive/test/process_replay/`): rather than only unit-testing individual functions, the project's primary regression-safety mechanism replays **real recorded driving logs** (`rlog` segments) through each actual daemon process and diffs the output messages against checked-in reference logs (`process_replay.py`, `test_processes.py`, `compare_logs.py`, `model_replay.py` for the neural-net specifically, `regen.py`/`regen_all.py`/`update_ci_routes.py` for regenerating reference logs when a change is intentional). This is how a change to, say, `controlsd.py`'s control law gets validated against dozens of real cars' worth of recorded driving without needing physical vehicles for every PR. `test_onroad.py` and `test_updated.py` (also under `selfdrive/test/`) cover full onroad-boot and OTA-update integration scenarios respectively.

**What appears well-covered** (per subsystem agents' direct findings): `VCruiseHelper` (`selfdrive/car/tests/test_cruise_speed.py`, though the PCM-cruise code path is explicitly marked untested — `# TODO: test pcmCruise`), the longitudinal-maneuver simulation suite (multiple `LongitudinalPersonality` × e2e/non-e2e combinations), athena's reconnect-timing behavior (`system/athena/tests/test_athenad_ping.py` asserts the ~21s onroad / ~60s offroad reconnect windows found in code), and `test_lateral_mpc.py` (the **only** runtime exerciser of `lat_mpc.py`'s `LateralMpc`, confirming it is unit-tested but not integration-tested since nothing in production calls it — see Dead Code below).

**What is confirmed NOT tested / weakly tested**: PCM-cruise path of `VCruiseHelper` (explicit TODO in test file); `keep_pulse_timer`'s `keepLeft`/`keepRight` branch in `desire_helper.py` (currently unreachable given the `DESIRES` table, so untestable as dead code); `MAX_VEL_ERR` constant's actual consumer (flagged as possibly-dead, meaning its behavior isn't exercised from within `selfdrive/controls`); the `pandad.cc`/`Panda` USB-layer thread-safety between the main recv thread and `can_send_thread` (no test found asserting this, flagged as *uncertain* by the car-interface agent, not merely untested but unverifiable from source alone without the USB layer).

## Security Analysis (cross-cutting rollup)

Distinguishing confirmed findings from design concerns, per the subsystem agents' direct source reading.

### The core safety model (confirmed, `docs/SAFETY.md` cross-checked against code)
openpilot's Python/C++ code is **not** the final safety authority for vehicle actuation — the **panda firmware** is (out of scope of this repo's Python/C++ code, lives in the vendored `panda`/`opendbc_repo` repos). Confirmed from `selfdrive/pandad/`: until `card.py` finishes fingerprinting (`FirmwareQueryDone`) and interface init (`ControlsReady`), every panda stays in an inert `ELM327` diagnostic safety mode (§Car Interface, `PandaSafety::fetchCarParams`) — no car-specific actuation is physically possible before that point regardless of what Python code does. Independently, `pandad.cc`'s `send_panda_states` forces `SafetyModel::NO_OUTPUT` whenever ignition is off or the device isn't onroad, **regardless of what `CarParams` last configured** — a second, redundant enforcement layer at the C++/firmware boundary, on top of whatever bounds-checking the firmware itself does on steering/gas/brake commands. This layered design (Python computes intent → C++ relays intent + independently enforces gross on/off state → firmware bounds-checks every individual command) is a genuine defense-in-depth pattern, confirmed across three independent code locations by the car-interface agent.

### Confirmed vulnerabilities / concerns

| Finding | Severity (assessed) | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **`webrtcd` binds `0.0.0.0:5001` with no authentication** | Design concern — real exposure if the device is reachable | `system/webrtc/webrtcd.py`, launched unconditionally (when `notcar` — i.e. sim/bench use, not real vehicles) by `system/manager/process_config.py:113`. A network-reachable peer can bridge arbitrary cereal services and publish messages via unchecked `type`/`data` fields in WebRTC data-channel payloads, per the system-services agent's direct reading. Mitigated in practice by only running when `notcar` is true (sim/dev contexts) and by the device typically being behind NAT/NAT+no-port-forward — but the daemon itself has no auth layer. |
| **`system/hardware/tici/id_rsa` — a private RSA key committed to the repo** | Confirmed intentional, not a leak | Documented in `docs/how-to/connect-to-comma.md:56` as the shared factory-default key for pre-provisioning SSH access before a device's real per-device key is generated in `/persist/`. Still worth flagging to anyone auditing the repo for committed secrets, since it is a real, functional private key in version control by design. |
| **openpilot's own OTA payload (`system/updated`) has no client-side signature check** | Design concern | Trust for the openpilot software payload itself rests on TLS only (git-fetch over HTTPS), confirmed by the system-services agent's direct reading of `system/updated/updated.py`. By contrast, the **AGNOS base-OS partition update** (`system/hardware/tici/agnos.py`) *does* perform full SHA-256/512 hash verification with a crash-safe "clear-hash-before-write" protocol — i.e. the base OS is defended more rigorously than the openpilot application layer sitting on top of it. |
| **Athena auth is sound asymmetric-crypto design** | Not a vulnerability — noted for completeness | Per-device RSA/ECDSA keypair, hourly-reminted JWTs signed client-side, server never sees the private key, connections are outbound-only (no inbound listening socket on the device for athena itself). Server-side verification logic is outside this repo and unverifiable from here. |
| **`sentry.py` includes dongle ID in crash reports** | Design concern (PII/device-tracking), gated | Only active for comma-origin registered devices (confirmed check in code) — not user-configurable forks, per the system-services agent. |
| **`deleter.py` has no upload-before-delete guarantee** | Design concern | Only respects lock/preserve xattrs, not upload completion status — a segment could theoretically be deleted before it's finished uploading under disk-pressure conditions (confirmed from code structure, not empirically reproduced). |
| **`can_capnp_to_list`'s unbounded traversal limit** | Minor/theoretical | `selfdrive/pandad/pandad_api_impl.py` decodes with `traversal_limit_in_words=NO_TRAVERSAL_LIMIT` — trusts the input size unconditionally. This is IPC between local trusted processes over the SHM bus, not network-facing, so practical exposure is minimal, but it's a real absence of a resource-exhaustion guard. |

### Design property, not a flaw
`Params`' file-per-key storage with a static registry (`common/params_keys.h`) rejecting unknown keys is a reasonable hardening choice — it prevents arbitrary key injection from ever being interpreted by any consumer, confirmed by the UI/common agent's direct reading of `params_pyx.pyx`.

## Performance Notes (cross-cutting rollup)

- **`card.py`'s `Ratekeeper` is monitoring-only, not pacing** (`selfdrive/car/card.py`, confirmed by the car-interface agent reading `card_thread()`): `rk.monitor_time()` is called, never `rk.keep_time()`/`keepTime()`. The loop's true cadence is entirely a function of incoming `can` message arrival rate (nominally 100 Hz from `pandad`), not an independent timer — a discrepancy from the in-code comment implying `Ratekeeper` enforces the 100 Hz rate the way it does in most other daemons (e.g. `pandad.cc`'s native loop, which *does* call `rk.keepTime()`).
- **One-frame actuation lag by design**: `card.py`'s `state_publish()` (publishes `carOutput`) runs before `controls_update()` (which computes the new actuator output) within the same `step()`, so the published `carOutput` always reflects the *previous* frame's actuator command — an intentional latency/ordering tradeoff to let downstream consumers start their own step as early as possible in the frame, per the in-code comment.
- **Longitudinal MPC uses a bounded-iteration real-time-iteration QP scheme** (`SQP_RTI`, `qp_solver_iter_max=10`, confirmed `selfdrive/controls/lib/longitudinal_mpc_lib/long_mpc.py`) specifically to guarantee fixed per-tick compute time rather than solving to full convergence — a deliberate real-time-safety-over-optimality tradeoff.
- **`torqued`'s fit uses total-least-squares via SVD** and **`lagd` uses masked FFT cross-correlation** (both confirmed by the localization agent) — both are $O(n \log n)$-or-better choices appropriate for the online/streaming context they run in, rather than naive iterative fits.
- **`camerad` is confirmed single-threaded, event-poll-driven** (`system/camerad/spectra.cc:249-311`, per the perception agent) rather than one-thread-per-camera, with zero-copy buffer publishing (VisionIPC) into shared memory — avoids per-frame copy overhead across the camera→modeld boundary.
- **Multi-core pinning is used pervasively on-device** (confirmed via `system/hardware/tici/hardware.py`'s `initialize_hardware`, and `common/realtime.py`'s `config_realtime_process` calls seen in nearly every daemon's `main()`): `card` pins to core 4, `radard`/`plannerd` to core 5 at low priority, `pandad`'s native loop to core 3 at realtime priority 54, the UI to core 5 — a manually curated CPU budget across the fixed embedded hardware rather than relying on the OS scheduler alone.

## Documentation vs. Code Discrepancies (rollup)

| Doc/comment claim | Actual code behavior | Where found |
|---|---|---|
| README: "upgrades the driver assistance system in **300+ supported cars**" | Same README, two paragraphs later, links "the **275+ supported cars**" (`docs/CARS.md`) | `README.md` (both instances) — internally inconsistent supported-car count, not resolvable from this repo alone (**uncertain** which figure is current; likely a stale edit) |
| Launch entry point implied to be `launch_openpilot.sh` | It's a 2-line trampoline to `launch_chffrplus.sh` (legacy name from comma's older "chffr"/"chffrplus" products), which contains all real logic including the OTA-apply step | `launch_openpilot.sh:1-3`, `launch_chffrplus.sh` |
| Implicit assumption (common in older openpilot docs/tutorials) that the on-road UI is Qt/QML | This fork's `selfdrive/ui/` is pure-Python + raylib (`pyray`); Qt/C++ only remains in `tools/cabana/` | `selfdrive/ui/ui.py`, `system/ui/lib/application.py` — full finding in UI section above |
| `docs/SAFETY.md` states driver monitoring and "excessive actuation checks" (`selfdrive/selfdrived/helpers.py`) must not be disabled/nerfed by forks | Code-level confirmation not separately re-audited in this pass beyond confirming the file exists and is in the pipeline (§Control Stack, `selfdrived`) — treated as a policy statement rather than a testable code claim | `docs/SAFETY.md` |
| `card.py` in-code comment: "card is driven by can recv, expected at 100Hz" | True in the sense that `can` arrives at ~100 Hz, but the phrasing could mislead a reader into thinking the `Ratekeeper(100, ...)` instance enforces that rate — it only monitors/logs lag (`monitor_time()`, never `keep_time()`) | `selfdrive/car/card.py` (§Car Interface, "Important nuance") |
| `desire_helper.py` living under `selfdrive/controls/lib/` implies it's consumed by the control-planning pipeline | Sole runtime importer is `selfdrive/modeld/modeld.py` — directory placement doesn't reflect actual ownership | `selfdrive/controls/lib/desire_helper.py` vs `selfdrive/modeld/modeld.py:26,306,342` |
| `selfdrive/locationd/`'s general framing (module docstrings) suggests a fuller sensor-fusion story | GPS daemons (`ubloxd`/`pigeond`/`qcomgpsd`) run completely independently, unconnected to `locationd`'s EKF, which fuses IMU + camera odometry only in this build | Localization section above |
| `calibrationd`'s docstring implies general roll/pitch/yaw calibration | Roll is explicitly hardcoded to zero in the implementation, not estimated | Localization section above |

## Unknowns / Open Questions

Honestly flagged rather than guessed, per items each subsystem agent explicitly could not resolve from static reading alone:

- Whether this checkout constitutes a meaningfully divergent fork of upstream `commaai/openpilot` or is a same-day mirror — **not a git repository here** (no `.git` directory), so no blame/history/diff-against-upstream was possible. The only distinguishing artifact found is the directory name itself.
- Exact mechanism of the `openpilot/` namespace-packaging shim (symlinks vs. `.pth` files vs. generated stubs) — inferred as a packaging shim from its 9KB size and mirrored subdirectory names, not individually verified file-by-file.
- Thread-safety of the `Panda`/`PandaCommsHandle` USB/SPI layer shared between `pandad.cc`'s main thread and `can_send_thread` — no explicit mutex was visible in the files read, and the underlying comms-handle implementation was out of this pass's scope, so safety "relies on" rather than "is proven by" what was read.
- The actual consumer of `/var/tmp/power_watchdog` (touched by `system/manager/manager.py`) — inferred to be an external power-management component, not found in this repo's scope.
- Where `HardwareBase.uninstall()`'s actual wipe logic executes — `system/hardware/tici/hardware.py`'s `uninstall()` only touches a marker file and reboots; the wipe presumably happens in an early-boot script not covered in this pass.
- Whether `MAX_VEL_ERR` (`selfdrive/controls/lib/drive_helpers.py`) has a live consumer somewhere outside `selfdrive/controls`' own scope, or is genuinely dead — flagged as possibly-dead, not confirmed either way.
- Server-side verification logic for athena JWTs and the openpilot software-update git-fetch trust chain — both anchor ultimately in comma's cloud infrastructure, outside this repository's contents.

## Code Modification Guide

Concrete "where do I touch this" guidance, derived from the traced data flow and confirmed call graphs above.

**To change how the car accelerates/brakes (longitudinal behavior)**
1. Tuning constants (comfortable accel, jerk cost, follow distance): `selfdrive/controls/lib/longitudinal_mpc_lib/long_mpc.py` (cost weights table, `get_T_FOLLOW`/`get_jerk_factor` for personality-based tuning).
2. Higher-level policy (when to allow throttle, turn-limiting, experimental-mode blending): `selfdrive/controls/lib/longitudinal_planner.py:update()`.
3. The actual PID/actuation loop that turns a target accel into a pedal command: `selfdrive/controls/controlsd.py` (`LongControl`, out of this doc's line-by-line scope but registered in the pipeline table).
4. If touching MPC internals, regenerate the acados C code via `long_mpc.py`'s `__main__` block, and update `selfdrive/test/process_replay` reference logs (`update_ci_routes.py`/`regen.py`) since this is exactly the kind of change process-replay is designed to catch.
5. Tests to update: `selfdrive/car/tests/test_cruise_speed.py` (maneuver simulations), `selfdrive/controls/tests/`.

**To change lane-centering / steering behavior** — note this is *not* where a naive directory search would suggest:
1. The actual path-planning logic lives inside the driving-policy **model** (`selfdrive/modeld/modeld.py`), not in `selfdrive/controls/lib/lateral_mpc_lib/` (confirmed dead) or a `lateral_planner.py` (doesn't exist in this fork). Changing planned-path behavior means retraining/replacing the model, not editing Python control code.
2. The low-level steering **controller** (PID/angle/torque, turning a commanded curvature into a steering actuator command) is in `selfdrive/controls/controlsd.py` (`LatControlPID`/`LatControlAngle`/`LatControlTorque`, selected in `Controls.__init__` based on `CP.steerControlType`/`lateralTuning`).
3. Safety-limiting of the model's raw curvature output: `selfdrive/controls/lib/drive_helpers.py:clip_curvature()`.
4. Lane-change trigger logic (turn-signal state machine): `selfdrive/controls/lib/desire_helper.py`, but remember it's driven from `modeld.py`, not `plannerd.py`.
5. Tests: `selfdrive/controls/tests/`, `selfdrive/car/tests/`.

**To add support for a new car**
1. Out of this document's exhaustive scope — lives in `opendbc_repo/opendbc/car/<brand>/` (DBC file, `carstate.py`, `carcontroller.py`, `interface.py`, `fingerprints.py`), following the `CarInterfaceBase`/`CarStateBase`/`CarControllerBase` pattern documented at interface level in the Car Interface section above (Toyota's `opendbc_repo/opendbc/car/toyota/interface.py` is the representative example referenced there).
2. `selfdrive/car/docs.py` / `CARS_template.md` regenerate the supported-cars documentation from `opendbc/car/docs.py` — run after adding a car.
3. Safety firmware changes (if the new car needs new CAN message bounds-checking) belong in `opendbc_repo/opendbc/safety/` — the actual final safety authority, per the Security section above.

**To change what gets logged / uploaded**
1. Segment recording: `system/loggerd/loggerd.cc` (native).
2. Upload triggering/retry policy: `system/loggerd/uploader.py`.
3. Deletion policy: `system/loggerd/deleter.py` (currently no upload-before-delete guarantee — see Security rollup — factor that in before changing retention windows).
4. New message types must be added to `cereal/log.capnp` first (schema-first — every publisher/subscriber consumes generated bindings from this file).

**To change remote-access / telemetry behavior**
1. `system/athena/athenad.py` (connection lifecycle, RPC handlers) — read the Auth/registration subsection above first; any change here has direct security implications (auth, exposed RPC surface).
2. Device registration: `system/athena/registration.py`, `common/api.py`.
3. Tests: `system/athena/tests/` (includes reconnect-timing assertions — a behavior change to keepalive tuning should update `test_athenad_ping.py`'s expected windows).

**To change process startup/shutdown behavior (which daemons run when)**
1. `system/manager/process_config.py` — add/modify a `procs` entry and its `should_run` predicate.
2. If the new predicate needs new state, it likely needs a new `Params` key (register it in `common/params_keys.h` first, or it will raise `UnknownKeyName` at runtime) or a new `CarParams`/`deviceState` field (schema-first change in `cereal/`).

**General cross-cutting rule confirmed throughout this document**: because every inter-process boundary is a cereal message, changing any message's schema (`cereal/log.capnp` or `car.capnp`, i.e. `opendbc_repo/opendbc/car/car.capnp` per the redirect noted in the UI section) is the correct **first** step before touching any producer/consumer code — capnp is the single source of truth for what data crosses a process boundary, and every subsystem section above was written by reading schema-driven message flow, not inferring it.

## Developer Quick Start

**Where to start reading**: this document's Entry Points section (§4) → the Car Interface section (simplest full pipeline slice: CAN in, `CarState` out, `CarControl` in, CAN out) → the Control Stack section (the actual driving-decision logic) → everything else as needed. Do not start with `system/` services; they're infrastructure, not driving logic.

**Most central files** (appear as dependencies of the most other subsystems, per the call/data-flow graphs above): `cereal/messaging/__init__.py` (`SubMaster`/`PubMaster` — used by literally every daemon), `common/params.py` (used by nearly every daemon for persistent state), `common/realtime.py` (`Ratekeeper`, `config_realtime_process` — used by every realtime loop), `cereal/log.capnp` + `opendbc_repo/opendbc/car/car.capnp` (the schemas that define every inter-process contract).

**Dangerous to modify without extreme care**: anything in the Car Interface / Control Stack chain (`selfdrive/car/`, `selfdrive/controls/`, `selfdrive/pandad/`, `opendbc_repo/opendbc/safety/`) — this is the actuation path; per `docs/SAFETY.md`, changes here are explicitly bound by ISO26262/MISRA-C-adjacent process expectations even though this repo's Python layer itself isn't MISRA-checked (only `opendbc/safety/` C firmware is, per that doc). `system/athena/` (remote access — auth/security surface). `system/updated/` (OTA — bricking risk).

**Safe/independent to modify**: `tools/` (dev tooling, no onroad safety implication), UI cosmetics in `selfdrive/ui/` (the raylib layer) as long as `latActive`/`enabled`/alert logic itself isn't touched, most of `common/` utility functions (verify call sites first since `Ratekeeper`/`params`/`transformations` are extremely widely used — a subtle regression there is high-blast-radius even though the *code* is simple).

**How to run it**: `bash <(curl -fsSL openpilot.comma.ai)` is the on-device install path (per README, unverified in this pass — no device available). For development, `tools/` contains `sim/` (CARLA bridge) and `replay/` (replays recorded `rlog` routes through the real daemons) — these are the two ways to exercise the pipeline without a car, per the UI/common/tools section above.

**How to debug it**: `cloudlog`/`swaglog` (`common/swaglog.py`) is the universal structured logger, all daemons bind `daemon=<name>` context to it; `tools/cabana` for CAN-level debugging (the one place Qt is still used); `tools/plotjuggler` for message-level plotting; `system/proclogd`/`system/statsd` for resource-usage introspection; Sentry (`system/sentry.py`) for crash reports (dongle-ID-tagged, comma-origin devices only).

**How to test changes**: unit tests via `pytest` (64 files across the tree, run per-subsystem or whole-tree); for anything touching a realtime daemon's message-level behavior, use `selfdrive/test/process_replay/` against recorded routes — this is the project's actual regression-safety net for driving behavior, not just unit tests.

**How to trace a feature through the code**: start from the `cereal/log.capnp` message it produces or consumes (every cross-process boundary is a named capnp message), grep for `PubMaster([...])`/`SubMaster([...])` calls naming it to find every producer/consumer, then read each in the order data actually flows (as diagrammed in each subsystem section's pipeline-position subsection above).

**Common pitfalls surfaced in this analysis**: assuming directory location implies ownership (`desire_helper.py`/`lat_mpc.py` under `controls/` are misleading — see Dead Code rollup); assuming `Ratekeeper` always paces a loop (it doesn't in `card.py` — see Performance notes); assuming the Python/C++ layer is the safety authority (it isn't — the panda firmware is, see Security rollup); assuming this fork has GPS-fused localization (it doesn't — `locationd` is IMU+vision only in this build).

**Important assumptions this document had to make explicit** (see Unknowns above): no git history was available to confirm fork provenance; some claims about server-side/cloud behavior (athena JWT verification, update-payload trust) are necessarily inferred from the device-side code's expectations, not confirmed against server code (which isn't in this repository).
